title: Exact Nonperturbative Equilibrium Mode Statistics in Nonlinear Wave and Lattice Systems
authors: Jialin Zhang, Yong Zhang, Hong Zhao
abstract: We derive exact finite-size nonperturbative representations of equilibrium modal occupations and related statistics for three representative nonlinear systems: the Majda-McLaughlin-Tabak dispersive-wave model, the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou beta anharmonic chain, and the discrete nonlinear Schrodinger lattice field. Independent simulations confirm the predictions from weak to strong nonlinearity. For DNLS, the theory remains accurate across the weak-coupling quasicondensation crossover, where large low-mode occupations and long-range coherence amplify interaction effects even when the bare nonlinear coefficient is small. The finite-ring DNLS occupations are further resolved into a positive sum of Rayleigh-Jeans channels with distinct correlation lengths, explaining when a single Rayleigh-Jeans law applies and why it fails near quasicondensation. In MMT and DNLS, the exact occupations also determine the mean modal frequencies even when the dynamical spectra broaden or split. The nonperturbative results allow a direct assessment of two representative perturbative approaches. Treating the mean interaction appropriately yields accurate low-order approximations, including at strong nonlinearity. At higher orders, however, the corrections cease to decrease and successive approximations oscillate with increasing amplitude; both finite-order approaches also fail near weak-coupling quasicondensation. Thus neither low-order agreement nor a small bare coupling guarantees a reliable perturbative description. The results establish nonperturbative equilibrium theory for widely used nonlinear wave and lattice models and provide a quantitative basis for modal distributions of energy, particles, and optical power in nonlinear optics, dispersive waves, anharmonic lattices, and cold-atom systems.
summary: This work establishes exact, nonperturbative equilibrium theories for modal statistics in nonlinear wave and lattice systems like DNLS and MMT. It rigorously proves that simple perturbative expansions fail under strong coupling or near quasicondensation. The findings provide a necessary quantitative basis for accurately describing energy and particle distributions in complex nonlinear physical systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to derive exact, nonperturbative representations for the equilibrium modal occupations and related statistics in various nonlinear wave and lattice systems.
main_result: Nonperturbative theory is crucial because standard perturbative methods fail near strong nonlinearity or in regimes like quasicondensation, where low-mode occupations amplify interaction effects.
method: The authors use the full Gibbs weight formalism to calculate thermal averages, comparing these exact results against various low-order perturbative expansions.
model_or_system: The study analyzes three representative nonlinear systems: the Majda-McLaughlin-Tabak (MMT) dispersive-wave model, the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou ($ eta$) anharmonic chain, and the Discrete Nonlinear Schrödinger (DNLS) lattice field.
key_observables: Equilibrium modal occupations ($\langle|a_k|^2angle$), mean modal frequencies, and the distribution of energy, particles, and optical power among modes.
important_parameters: The analysis covers regimes from weak to strong nonlinearity, with special focus on the quasicondensation crossover in the DNLS model.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the full Gibbs weight calculation yields the exact nonperturbative result, contrasting with the limitations of low-order approximations.
figures_summary: Figures compare finite-N theory against Metropolis MC simulations for MMT occupations, and show the failure of Hartree/Rayleigh-Jeans relations near quasicondensation.
paper_structure: The paper systematically derives exact formulas for modal statistics in MMT and FPUT, then applies the framework to DNLS, culminating in a detailed comparison demonstrating the failure of perturbative methods at higher orders.
why_interesting: The rigorous demonstration of when and why simple approximations fail in nonlinear systems provides a crucial theoretical benchmark for modeling energy transport and coherence in nonlinear optics and lattice dynamics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Nonperturbative equilibrium occupations of two branches of the finite- mode MMT family. Here and below, MMT1 and MMT2 denote branches I and II, respectively. Panels (a,b) show the purely quartic branch and panels (c,d) the mixed cubic-quartic branch for M = 8, T = 1, and bT = 10 or 100. Solid curves are the complete finite-M nonperturbative predictions; symbols are independent Metropolis MC simulations of the original Hamiltonian, with replica standard errors.

Figure 2: Finite-size nonperturbative spectrum of the fixed-boundary FPUT-β chain for N = 16, T = 1, and bT = 30 or 70. Solid curves are the exact finite- N constrained-bond predictions, and symbols are independent MC data in the original displacement variables, with replica standard errors.

Figure 3: DNLS occupations in the normal regime for T = 1, µ = −0.2, L = 256, and b = 3 or 20. The upper panels show n(q) against wave number. The lower panels show 1/n(q) against the bare lattice frequency. Solid curves are the exact finite-ring nonperturbative predictions, and symbols are independent MC data with replica standard errors.

Figure 4: Finite-size DNLS quasicondensation at T = 1 and L = 256. (a) Zero- mode fraction f0 = n0/ P k nk versus chemical potential for b = 0.1, 0.2, 1, and 10. (b) The same data plotted against µ/b. Solid curves are the exact finite-ring transfer-operator predictions and symbols are independent MC results.

Figure 5: Cumulative-channel reconstruction of the exact finite-ring DNLS in- verse spectrum at T = 1, L = 256, and b = 0.1, plotted against ω(0) k = 2 −2 cos qk. Channels are ranked by decreasing Θ(L) c . The black curve is the exact sum over all retained channels; colored curves are the inverses of the cu- mulative occupations from the leading 1, 2, 4, and 8 channels. (a) µ = 2. (b) µ = 10. Successive cumulative sums reconstruct the complete occupation. Their different slopes mainly show the spectral weight added by successive channels; the weaker curvature of the full inverse spectrum is quantified by Eq. (75).
